Creep and solifluction are slow mass movements. Mudflow (a rapid flow) and slump (a landslide-type movement) are classed as rapid movements.

Stratovolcanoes (composite cones) are tall, steep cones of alternating layers of viscous felsic or intermediate lava and ash. Felsic magma traps large amounts of gas under pressure, so their eruptions are often explosive.

Potholes form when pebbles and boulders caught in eddies swirl round and grind the stream bed, which is abrasion (corrasion). Attrition is the wearing down of the load particles themselves, corrosion is solution, and solifluction is a mass movement, not a river process.

Spindle fibres attach to the kinetochores, disc-shaped protein structures on the centromere of each chromosome. Telomeres are the chromosome ends and centrioles are organelles that organise the spindle, not parts of the chromosome.

The sodium-calcium exchanger moves Na+ into the cell and Ca2+ out of it, two ions in opposite directions across the membrane, which is antiport. Symport moves both the same way and uniport moves a single species.

Complex tissues are made of more than one cell type; xylem (tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and fibres) is one. Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma are simple tissues of one cell type.
Apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots divide continually and increase the length of the plant. Collenchyma, endodermis and cortex are permanent tissues or regions.

The coronary arteries branch from the aorta and supply oxygenated blood to the heart muscle. The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs, the renal artery to the kidneys and the hepatic artery to the liver.

Mammals (and birds) have a four-chambered heart with complete separation, so blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: double circulation. Fishes have single circulation, and amphibians have only incomplete double circulation with mixing in a single ventricle.
Cholesterol is a sterol, a steroid lipid found in cell membranes and used to make steroid hormones and bile acids.
Xerophytes are plants adapted to dry habitats. Mesophytes grow in moderate moisture, hydrophytes in water and halophytes in saline soils.
